passage: Rain kept the kindergarten indoors, so twenty children played musical statues in a room meant for ten. Pallavi, five, spun with her arms wide, then pulled them in when her elbow brushed Mridul. When the music stopped, she froze on one foot, wobbling, and put a hand on the wall instead of grabbing him. Mridul was hugging everyone who froze near him. A boy squirmed away. Pallavi said, "He doesn't want a hug. Ask first." Mridul let go and froze with his hands on his own knees.

qa.q: What game were the children playing?
qa.a: They were playing musical statues.

qa.q: Why might Pallavi have pulled her arms in after brushing Mridul?
qa.a: She noticed she had touched him and seemed to want to keep out of the other children's space in the crowded room.

qa.q: How could the teacher make the game safer in a crowded room?
qa.a: She could mark a spot for each child with tape or chalk and remind everyone to ask before touching.

qa.q: What was it like for the boy who squirmed away?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable being hugged, and Pallavi's words helped his wish to be noticed without him having to shout.

grounding: It shows a child keeping balance, protecting others' space and speaking up for a peer's body boundary during an active game.

passage: In the colony park in Hyderabad, Lakshmi and Uday were playing hopscotch on squares chalked by the watchman's son. Lakshmi hopped to seven on one foot, arms out like wings, then tipped and landed with both feet down. "Again!" she said. When Uday's turn came he started hopping right behind her. "Wait, I'm too near," Lakshmi said, stepping back so he wouldn't crash into her. Later a girl tugged Lakshmi's plait to tease her. "Don't pull my hair, it hurts," Lakshmi said. The girl let go and said sorry.

qa.q: Which square did Lakshmi reach before she tipped over?
qa.a: She hopped to square seven before she tipped.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi thinking when she said, "Wait, I'm too near"?
qa.a: She seemed to realise they might collide and wanted to give Uday room to hop safely.

qa.q: How could an adult support Lakshmi when someone pulls her hair?
qa.a: Praise her clear words and back her up calmly, while helping the other child practise asking before touching.

qa.q: How did the girl who pulled the plait learn something here?
qa.a: Hearing "it hurts" directly showed her the tease was not fun for Lakshmi, so she stopped and said sorry.

grounding: It shows a child balancing in a hopping game, keeping safe distance and stating her own body boundary.

passage:
"Tickle monster!" Tushar pounced, fingers wiggling.
Nikita shrieked, then went stiff. "Stop. Stop, Tushar."
He froze, hands in the air. "But you were laughing."
"Now I'm not."
Papa looked up from his tea. "What did she say?"
"Stop," Tushar mumbled, shuffling back. "Can I tickle your feet only?"
"No. But we can do the pillow jump."
"Okay! You go first. I'll stand back here so you don't land on me."
Nikita bounced off the sofa cushion, wobbled and caught her balance.
"Wow, you didn't fall!" Tushar cheered.

qa.q: What game did Nikita suggest instead of tickling?
qa.a: She suggested the pillow jump.

qa.q: Why did Tushar say "But you were laughing"?
qa.a: He was confused, because laughing looked like fun to him, and he may have felt a little stung at being stopped.

qa.q: What would you advise Tushar about tickling next time?
qa.a: Ask first, and stop the moment someone says stop, even if they were laughing a second ago.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita when Tushar freezes at once?
qa.a: She learns her "stop" is respected, which likely makes her happy to keep playing with him.

grounding: It shows siblings honouring a spoken body boundary and giving each other space to balance in active play.

passage:
Coach's note, Saturday sports hour, Lokesh Sir
Pema did well on the balance beam today, arms out, eyes on the far end. In 'traffic lights' she stopped when a slower child was in front of her instead of pushing through. When the group was making a circle, she asked her neighbour, 'Can I hold your hand?' and waited for a nod. I pointed this out to the group. 👍

qa.q: What did Pema do when a slower child was in front of her?
qa.a: She stopped instead of pushing through.

qa.q: What does Pema waiting for a nod suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she understood that her neighbour's hand and body belong to them, so she wanted permission first.

qa.q: How could Lokesh Sir help the other children learn from Pema?
qa.a: He could make asking before touching part of every circle game, praising children when they do it.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel being asked before their hand is held?
qa.a: They would likely feel respected and comfortable, since they got a choice.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping balance, managing personal space and respecting peers' bodily boundaries.

passage: After the rice harvest, the children raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields. Baljeet ran with arms out like wings, wobbling but never falling in. When Kunal tripped ahead of her, she slowed and leaned sideways so she wouldn't bump him. Later, playing train, Kunal said, 'Don't pull my shirt, it hurts.' Baljeet let go and held his shoulders lightly instead. 'Choo-choo,' she said.

qa.q: Where did the children race after the harvest?
qa.a: They raced along the narrow mud bunds between fields.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet let go of Kunal's shirt?
qa.a: She understood he did not like it and cared that she was hurting him, so she changed how she held on.

qa.q: What could an older cousin do to support this kind of play?
qa.a: They could praise Baljeet for listening and remind all children to check before grabbing each other in games.

qa.q: What would change if Baljeet had ignored Kunal's words?
qa.a: Kunal might feel hurt and not want to play, and the game could turn into a fight.

grounding: Shows a child balancing in active play and respecting a peer's body when asked, in a rural setting.
